blocks.content: ADD does everything COPY does, plus two extra tricks: it can automatically extract local tar archives, and it can fetch files directly from a remote URL.

Point ADD at a local .tar, .tar.gz, or similar archive, and it automatically extracts the contents into the destination, no separate tar command needed. It can also take a URL directly and download the file into the image.

blocks.alt: Auto-extraction and remote URLs, on top of a plain copy

blocks.content:
ADD app.tar.gz /app/
# Automatically extracts app.tar.gz into /app/
ADD https://example.com/file.txt /data/
# Downloads the file directly into the image

blocks.content: 2. Why It Is Used More Carefully Than COPY
blocks.text: 2. Why It Is Used More Carefully Than COPY

blocks.content: The URL-fetching behavior in particular is a real caveat: the fetched content is not checksummed against anything by default, and it depends on the remote URL staying available and unchanged, an outside dependency baked directly into your build's reproducibility.

blocks.alt: A remote fetch with no built-in integrity check

blocks.content: Docker's own documentation, and most teams' style guides, recommend defaulting to COPY for ordinary file copying, and reaching for ADD only when you specifically need its extraction or URL-fetching behavior, not as a general substitute for COPY.

blocks.alt: COPY as the default, ADD only when its extras are needed

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: ADD extends COPY with automatic archive extraction and remote URL fetching, capabilities plain COPY does not have.
Default to COPY for ordinary file copying, its behavior is simpler and more predictable, reach for ADD only when you specifically need its extras.
